newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK shipping magnate urged to declare leadership bid.
newsitem.headline: HK shipping magnate urged to declare leadership bid.

text.p: A Hong Kong billionaire, tipped as front-runner to lead the territory after its return to Chinese rule next year, was under pressure on Thursday to end his silence and declare whether or not he will run for the job.

Interest in shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa has intensified following the controversial nomination as candidate of the British colony's chief justice, Sir Ti Liang Yang, in what had previously been regarded as a one-horse race.
Tung, despite his reticence, had been widely touted as communist China's choice to take over when the British furl the flag and depart at midnight next June 30, now 299 days away.

"Time is running short so I hope Mr Tung will make a firm decision in a very short while," said businessman Vincent Lo, a member of the China-picked Preparatory Committee responsible for implementing the transition after more than 150 years of British rule.
"Mr Tung obviously is a popular candidate and if he is prepared to declare his candidacy I am sure he will have a lot of support," Lo added.
A pro-democracy legislator who spoke to Tung on Wednesday said the 58-year-old tycoon had quizzed him on grass roots social and political issues.
"I have the impression that he (Tung) may be interested in running," legislator Tsang Kin-shing told reporters after the meeting.

Tung was not available for comment. He left for Beijing on Wednesday, sparking off speculation he wanted to tap Chinese officials for their views on Yang's bid for power, the Oriental Daily News said on Thursday.

Preparatory Committee members are holding discussions in Beijing to hammer out the mechanisms for choosing a 400-strong Selection Committee responsible for naming Hong Kong's post-colonial leader before a November deadline.
Nominations to the Selection Committee end on September 14. So far, almost 20,000 nomination forms have been distributed and 429 completed forms returned.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby has denounced the selection process as a sham, arguing the committee will serve merely to rubber-stamp China's chosen candidate.
They say they believe Chinese president Jiang Zemin signalled Beijing's choice when he singled Tung out from a roomful of prominent Hong Kong advisers in January and pointedly shook his hand.
In regular opinion polls conducted by Hong Kong newspapers, the 67-year-old chief justice has won higher ratings that Tung.

Both men lag the head of the Hong Kong civil service, Anson Chan, Governor Chris Patten's deputy, but her close association with the British administration is widely regarded as ruling her out in Beijing's eyes.
Hong Kong newspaper editorials say there is a certain reluctance to seeing a powerful tycoon occupying the top spot.

Rival tycoons on the preparatory committee had also hinted they would be reluctant to see a businessman in such a powerful role and have endorsed Yang's bid, the Chinese language Tin Tin Daily reported from Beijing.
Yang however has opponents, particularly among the pro-democracy lobby who argue he lacks administrative experience.
Lawyers and pro-democracy politicians attacked him last November after he said the Bill of Rights, which China plans to dilute next year, had sown chaos in the judiciary.
